newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: China raises diesel, gasoline output by over 3 pct.
newsitem.headline: China raises diesel, gasoline output by over 3 pct.

text.p: China is expected to increase its production of diesel, gasoline and jet-kerosene fuel by slightly over three percent in 1997, Chinese industry sources said on Wednesday.
"We are boosting our runs in the catalytic crackers after the old ones have been debottlenecked and new ones have come onstream," a source at state refiner Sinopec said.

Chinese industry sources said the increase in output from the catalytic crackers, the second stage of refining crude oil, will raise its light products yield, or its output of diesel, gasoline and jet-kerosene fuel.
Sources at Sinopec's coastal refineries said the aim was to produce more diesel, which makes up 60 percent of China's total oil product imports.

"With oil demand expected to rise at a conservative estimate of five percent (a year) based on economic growth of eight percent for this year, we have to increase our diesel output," said the Sinopec source.
Chinese trade sources said while China will absorb the higher diesel and jet-kerosene fuel supplies, the surplus gasoline will be partly sold in the domestic market while the rest will be exported.
"High octane gasoline will be exported, the low octane supplies will be sold in the domestic market," a Chinese refiner said.
But the increase in light products yield is at the expense of fuel oil output.
"As fuel oil is fed into the catalytic crackers to produce more of the light products, China is expected to import more fuel oil to cover for the shortfall," a Chinese refiner said.

Traders said China's fuel oil output which totalled 23 million tonnes in 1996, a 17.45-percent drop from 1995 and the rise in diesel output by around 10 percent to 41 million tonnes reflected the change in production pattern.
China produced 30.5 million tonnes of gasoline in 1996.
In 1997, Chinese fuel oil imports are expected to exceed last year's 8.54 million tonnes, Chinese importers said.
China has been increasingly importing more of its oil product needs from South Korea and Japan.
Sources from state trader Sinochem in Hong Kong said freight costs between China and Singapore are assessed at $7.00-$8.00 per tonne compared with the $5.00-$6.00 from Japan/South Korea to Shanghai.
